zero_omission_notes.summary: This chapter covers the post-Mauryan era (c. 200 BCE to 300 CE), known as the 'Age of Reorganisation'. Following the fall of the Mauryas, India did not collapse into chaos; instead, regional powers reorganized and flourished across the subcontinent. Key dynasties include the Shungas and Chedis (Kharavela of Kalinga) in north/east India, the Satavahanas (Gautamiputra Satakarni) in the Deccan, the Kushanas (Kanishka) in the northwest, and the Sangam Era kingdoms (Cholas, Cheras, Pandyas) in the South. Overseas and overland trade (Silk Route, maritime Indian Ocean trade with the Roman Empire) reached new heights. A major cultural confluence occurred as foreign groups (Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Kushanas) adopted Indian religions (Buddhism, Hinduism), contributing to Gandhara and Mathura schools of art and Sanskrit literature.

detailed_sections.full_notes: Post-Mauryan fragmentation gave birth to strong regional kingdoms. Pushyamitra Shunga founded the Shunga dynasty in central India. King Kharavela of Chedi rule developed Kalinga. Satavahanas ruled the Deccan, issuing ship-motif coins indicating maritime prowess.

margin_notes_and_sidebars.title: J.C. Bose Quote (1917)
margin_notes_and_sidebars.content: By continuous living tradition and rejuvenescence, this land has readjusted itself through unnumbered transformations.

detailed_sections.section_number_and_title: 6.2 The Satavahanas & Sangam Age in South India
detailed_sections.full_notes: Satavahanas (capitals Amaravati and Pratishthana) controlled trade from coast to coast. Gautamiputra Satakarni revived Satavahana glory. Kings used matronymics (names derived from mothers, e.g. Gautamiputra). In deep South, Tamil Sangam literature documented the Cholas (King Karikala), Cheras, and Pandyas, their vibrant pearl trade, and poets' assemblies in Madurai.

margin_notes_and_sidebars.title: Matronymic Titles
margin_notes_and_sidebars.content: Satavahana rulers prefixing mother's name (Gautamiputra = son of Gautami) showed high respect for maternal lineage.

detailed_sections.section_number_and_title: 6.3 Kushanas, Silk Route & Schools of Art
detailed_sections.full_notes: Kushanas (under Kanishka) controlled key sections of the Silk Route connecting China, India, and Rome. Kanishka issued gold coins depicting Buddha and Shiva. Cultural synthesis created Gandhara Art (Greco-Buddhist style with realistic drapery/facial features) and Mathura Art (indigenous red sandstone sculptures).

margin_notes_and_sidebars.title: Naneghat Cave Inscriptions
margin_notes_and_sidebars.content: Naneghat caves near Pune served as toll collection points and rest houses for ancient trade caravans.

master_glossary_units_and_formulas.definition_or_meaning: The post-Mauryan historical period (200 BCE–300 CE) marked by regional state formation, vibrant international trade, and rich cultural synthesis.
An ancient body of Tamil poetry composed during assemblies (Sangams) of scholars and poets in Madurai, depicting social life, love, war, and trade.
Gandhara: Greco-Roman influence, grey schist stone, realistic features. Mathura: Indigenous Indian style, spotted red sandstone, spiritual expression.

textbook_exercises.question: Why was the post-Maurya era also known as the era of reorganisation?
textbook_exercises.answer: Because the end of centralized Mauryan rule led not to decay, but to the reorganization of powerful regional kingdoms across India. These kingdoms established flourishing trade networks, minted distinct coins, fostered art and literature, and assimilated foreign influxes into Indian culture.

textbook_exercises.question: Which rulers mentioned in this chapter included their mother's name in their title, and why did they do so?
textbook_exercises.answer: The Satavahana rulers (e.g., Gautamiputra Satakarni, Vashishtiputra Pulumavi) included matronymics. They did so to honor their mothers and highlight maternal lineage dignity in public governance.

short_answer_questions.question: Write a short note on Sangam literature.
short_answer_questions.answer: Sangam literature consists of ancient Tamil poems compiled across three scholarly assemblies (Sangams) in Madurai. It offers vivid insights into Sangam society, heroic kings (Cholas, Cheras, Pandyas), agricultural life, and bustling port cities like Kaveripattanam.

comprehensive_long_answers.question: How did foreign ruling groups like the Indo-Greeks, Shakas, and Kushanas assimilate into Indian society?
comprehensive_long_answers.answer: 1. Religious Adoption: Foreign rulers embraced Indian faiths—Heliodorus (Indo-Greek) erected a Garuda pillar to Vishnu; Kanishka (Kushana) patronized Buddhism. 2. Coinage & Language: They issued coins with Brahmi/Kharosthi legends alongside Greek, portraying Indian deities (Shiva, Buddha). 3. Artistic Synthesis: Fused Hellenistic realistic art styles with Indian iconography, developing Gandhara art. 4. Cultural Confluence: Adopted Indian names, royal customs, and married into local families, becoming integral to Indian society.

What historical evidence confirms this Roman trade?
qa.answer: Hoards of Roman gold coins found in South India and references in Sangam literature/Roman texts.

common_misconceptions_and_pitfalls.common_error_or_misconception: Viewing the post-Mauryan era as a 'Dark Age' of political collapse.
common_misconceptions_and_pitfalls.correct_fact_or_method: Emphasize that it was a period of immense economic prosperity, international trade growth, artistic innovation, and regional state maturity.
